opus-5.5.text:
I think that year was actually very valuable, even though at the time I didn't fully appreciate it. Before going abroad, I was just a student. I had studied, I had done some coursework and small projects, but I didn't really know how things work in the real world. Working as an engineer for a year gave me a very different perspective.

First, it taught me what it means to build something that has to actually work. In school, if your code runs once and gives you the result for your report, you're done. In industry, it has to be robust, other people have to use it, and you have to think about deadlines, about cooperation with teammates, about what the product really needs. That sense of engineering discipline stayed with me. Even later, when I was doing research, I always cared whether the method could really be implemented and scaled, not just whether it looked good on paper.

Second, it helped me figure out what I wanted. After working for a while, I realized that I was more excited about the open-ended questions, the things nobody knew how to solve yet, than about executing on well-defined tasks. That's a big reason I decided to go to the U.S. for a PhD. If I had gone straight from school, I might not have been so clear about why I was doing it. Having that year, I went with a stronger motivation, and when the PhD got hard, which it always does, I knew this was the path I had chosen deliberately.

And third, honestly, it made me more mature as a person. You learn how to communicate, how to handle pressure, how to take responsibility. Those soft skills matter a lot, whether you are in a research lab or in a company like NVIDIA, where research and engineering are so tightly connected.

So I wouldn't call it a detour. I think it was a foundation. Sometimes young people feel they have to rush to the next step, but a bit of real-world experience can make the next step much more meaningful.

fable-5.1.text:
That year taught me something no classroom could have. After I finished my master's in Taiwan, I spent a year working as an engineer before heading to the US for my PhD, and I think it was one of the most important years of my career, even though at the time it felt like a detour.

The biggest thing I learned was what engineering actually is. In school you solve problems that someone has already defined for you. The problem is clean, the data is clean, and there's a right answer at the back of the book. In a real engineering job, nobody hands you the problem. You have to figure out what the problem even is, and then you discover that the hardest part is rarely the algorithm. It's the messy data, the constraints you didn't anticipate, the fact that something has to actually work reliably for a customer and not just once in a demo. That mindset stayed with me. Even now, when I think about research, I always ask: can this actually be built, and will it hold up when real people use it?

The second thing was humility. I came out of my master's thinking I knew quite a bit. Then I worked with senior engineers who had been doing this for fifteen, twenty years, and I realized how much tacit knowledge exists that you can't get from papers. How to debug systematically, how to scope a project, how to communicate with people who don't share your background. That's craft, and craft takes time.

And honestly, the third thing is that it clarified why I wanted to do a PhD at all. When you're working on products, you see where the technology falls short. You see the walls. And I kept running into problems where I thought, there should be a better way to do this, but nobody knows how yet. That frustration is what pushed me toward research. I didn't go to the US because it was the expected next step. I went because I had specific questions I wanted answered, and I knew that industry at that time wasn't going to let me chase them.

So if a young person asked me whether they should go straight to a PhD or work first, I'd usually say work first, at least for a bit. You'll be a better researcher for it, because you'll know what matters.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses identifying undefined problems and handling messy data and constraints, but does not state that finding problems in a large software stack trains patience.

astra-6.text: That year gave me a practical perspective. In school, you often work on a problem that’s already clearly defined. In engineering, part of the work is figuring out what the problem actually is, what constraints matter, and whether your solution is useful. I think that was valuable preparation for going to the United States: it helped me connect what I wanted to learn with problems I might actually solve.

r001.rationale: The response says engineering involves figuring out the problem and its constraints, but does not mention patience or finding problems within a large software stack.

sol-6.1.text: I think the biggest value was learning how to turn an idea into something that actually works. In school, a problem usually has a fairly clear definition. In engineering, you have to figure out what the problem is, work within constraints, and keep going when your first solution fails. That year gave me a more practical mindset, which was useful when I later went to the United States to do research.

r001.rationale: The response says engineering involved figuring out the problem and persisting when a solution failed, but it does not mention a large software stack or state that finding problems in one trains patience.
